It's a policy and evidence initiative built on the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, seen from Pennsylvania. Every step from here appears in this changelog first. Read the full story What this initiative is for The Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA) is a federal law from 1993. It says the government may not substantially burden a person's sincere exercise of religion unless it can show a compelling reason, pursued in the least restrictive way. In 2006 the Supreme Court applied it to a church's sacramental tea. The library's first explainer walks through both.

items.s: What the Religious Freedom Restoration Act says, where it came from, how the Supreme Court applied it to a sacramental tea, and why sincerity sits at the center. A draft, to be reviewed.
items.x: TL;DR: RFRA is a 1993 federal law. If the federal government substantially burdens a person's sincere exercise of religion, it has to show that doing so serves a compelling interest in the least restrictive way, and it has to show that for the particular person, not just in general. In 2006 the Supreme Court unanimously applied that rule to a religious society's sacramental tea. RFRA doesn't legalize anything by itself: each claim is decided on its own facts, and sincerity comes first.
